candidates.rationale: An accelerating rise in a stock's percentile rank within its own 21-day range, confirmed by unusually high relative dollar volume, signals a participation-backed breakout that trend-following flow keeps pushing over the next few days rather than a thin, easily-reversed drift.

Ranking a stock's own 10-day change in intraday highs against its own trailing 63-day history of such changes isolates buying-pressure thrusts that are unusual for that specific stock's regime, giving volatility-adjusted momentum without an explicit std-dev division.

An open printing well above or below the prior session's low is a concrete overnight imbalance relative to where sellers previously stopped, and when it coincides with unusually high relative volume it reads as a crowded, over-extended reaction likely to partially fade over the next day.

An open sitting high in its own 15-day distribution of opens, combined with trading activity elevated relative to the stock's own 42-day norm, flags conviction buying arriving before the session even starts, which keeps feeding through over the next few days.

How much a stock's percentile position inside its own 15-day range has swung over the past 42 days proxies unresolved investor disagreement, distinct from raw price volatility since it is bounded by the stock's own range; paired with heavy relative volume that contested repricing keeps discounting the name until it resolves.

An accelerating rise in a high-ROA firm's percentile rank within its own 15-day range over just 3 days is more likely the market re-rating real earnings power than noise, so quality names breaking toward new local highs keep drifting up while the same move in low-ROA names tends to fade.

High-ROE firms whose open sits near the top of their own 21-day distribution of opens show informed demand arriving before the session starts in names the market already has structural (profitability) reason to favor, predicting continued outperformance.

Ranking a stock's own roughly five-month price change against its own multi-quarter history of such moves isolates repricings unusual even for that name, and sustained relative volume over the same broad window marks it as genuine institutional repositioning that persists for months.

Isolating only sharp negative 3-day price moves and weighting the drop by the stock's relative volume rank targets forced or panic selling specifically in liquid names, which tends to be absorbed and partially reverse, unlike a same-size drop in an illiquid name that is more likely information-driven and persists.

A short 5-day burst in a stock's own 63-day range-position is scaled down when its opening price's own positional rank has been erratic over the last 10 days, so the factor rewards the same-size move more when the trend is orderly rather than already whipsawing.

prompt:
You are proposing quantitative factor expressions for US large-cap equities.

Universe and data
- S&P 500 point-in-time constituents, roughly 500 names per day.
- Daily bars only, plus point-in-time quarterly fundamentals stamped from the
  report date. Every field is referenced with a leading `$`:
    $open $high $low $close $adj_close $volume $dollar_volume $return
    $roa $roe $operating_margin $leverage $asset_turnover
    $book_per_share $earnings_per_share $accrual_gap
  A bare name such as `close` is not a field and will be rejected.
- Execution convention: the signal is computed after the close of day T and the
  position is entered at the open of T+1.
- The window these factors are fitted and judged on runs from 2000 to 2013.
  Do not reason about anything later; you will never be shown a number from
  outside that window.

Syntax
- Operators are function calls: TS_MEAN, TS_STD, TS_MAX, TS_MIN, TS_RANK,
  TS_DELTA, TS_CORR, TS_COV, TS_SUM, TS_PRODUCT, TS_ARGMAX, TS_ARGMIN,
  TS_DECAY_LINEAR, EMA, DELAY, DELTA, RANK, ZSCORE, CS_RANK, CS_ZSCORE,
  CS_DEMEAN, IF, IF_ELSE, MIN, MAX, ABS, SIGN, LOG, LN, SQRT, POWER, BOUND,
  COUNT.
- Lookback windows must be positive integer literals, e.g. TS_MEAN($close, 21).
- Guard every division with a small epsilon: `/ (TS_STD($close, 21) + 1e-8)`.
- Well-formed example: -RANK(TS_CORR(RANK($close), RANK($volume), 5))

Hard limits every proposal must satisfy, or it is rejected before it is scored
- at most 200 characters
- at most 5 distinct `$fields`
- at most 4 free numeric constants (lookback windows and
  the 1e-8 epsilon guard do not count)
- expression tree depth at most 6
- must not share a complete sub-expression of 4 or more
  nodes with any published Alpha101 formula, or with any factor already in the
  archive. Restating a published alpha is the one thing that is always rejected.
- must cover at least 90% of the panel
- absolute rank correlation below 0.80 against every archive member

Output
- Return valid JSON only, matching the supplied JSON schema. No prose outside it.

  3. A raw $volume <-> $dollar_volume swap inside an otherwise-identical ratio/TS_MEAN shape still collapses (rho 0.963 this round); stop using that swap alone as a decorrelation technique.

The strongest accepts this round crossed a two-fundamental product ($operating_margin * $accrual_gap) against a $dollar_volume magnitude or delta term (fitness 2.3-3.9, niches slow/mixed/low and slow/fundamental/low); this fundamental-product-times-volume-magnitude family is validated and worth extending to other fundamental pairs.
  5. 5 of 20 rejects (25%) were exact same-run duplicates (two close/TS_MIN($low) range-position variants, two eps/book_per_share ratio restatements) -- dedupe the batch against itself before submitting; this is the largest rejection cause three rounds running.
  6. Swapping only the fundamental in a fixed RANK(fundamental) - RANK(price-ratio) template doesn't dodge archive_subtree: roe, accrual_gap, and operating_margin all failed this round against an eps-anchored parent, sharing 8-10 nodes each. Change the price-ratio branch or the combinator, not just the fundamental leaf.
  7. A DELAY(1)-lagged open/low/high ratio hit alpha101_subtree against a second, different Alpha101 formula beyond the well-known (high-low) chassis. Any ratio built purely from OHLC fields plus DELAY(.,1) is high risk -- mix in volume or a fundamental instead.
  8. Fundamental x fundamental (operating_margin*accrual_gap over a range guard, |t| 0.94), fundamental x price-rank-delta (|t| 0.27), and fundamental x extremum-position-difference (|t| 0.87) all missed cheap_screen this round -- pair a fundamental with a magnitude/volume/range leg instead.
  9. Swapping only the normalizing OHLC field inside a range ratio (rho 0.965, even with a window change too) or only the volume-transform LOG vs TS_RANK inside a ratio denominator (rho 0.981, same window) doesn't decorrelate -- change the numerator's structure, not just what normalizes it.
  10. Downside/upside return-volatility ratios (|t| 0.22) and price-range-vs-volume-delta correlations (|t| 0.18) were this round's weakest cheap_screen misses -- both remain low-probability shapes here.
  11. A 252-day TS_RANK($close) spread failed coverage at exactly 0.874, matching prior 252-day price attempts regardless of the expression wrapped around them -- treat 252 days as a hard coverage ceiling for price windows, not just fundamentals.
  12. The round's two best accepts (fitness 5.470 and 3.867) both crossed a fundamental-or-extremum magnitude leg with a volume-rank or short summed-range normalizer, not two directional/return legs -- keep favoring that magnitude-times-normalizer shape.
